name: Combinatorics
quick: The study of finite choices, arrangements, and counts.
definition: A counting argument specifies one outcome, explains which descriptions count as the same outcome, and counts each intended outcome once.
example: Choosing a committee and assigning named offices use different outcomes even with the same people.
confusion: The numbers alone do not determine the formula.

name: Sum principle
quick: Add counts of disjoint alternative categories.
definition: If categories partition the desired outcomes, the total is the sum of their sizes. Categories must not overlap.
example: Choose one soup or one sandwich from 4 soups and 6 sandwiches: 10 outcomes.
confusion: Choosing one of each is a product problem.

name: Product principle
quick: Multiply fixed numbers of choices at successive stages.
definition: The number of choices at each stage must be the stated number after every permitted earlier history. Actual options may vary while their count stays constant.
example: Two distinct letters from five give $5\cdot4=20$ ordered strings.
confusion: If branch counts differ, sum the appropriate branches instead.

name: Decision tree
quick: A branching drawing of choices leading to complete outcomes.
definition: A node records a partial choice, each outgoing branch a permitted next choice, and each leaf a completed outcome. A unique root-to-leaf route identifies one sequence of choices.
example: A branch with 3 completions and a separate branch with 5 give 8 outcomes.
confusion: The drawing is useful only if its branches cover the intended choices exactly.

name: Complementary counting
quick: Count all outcomes and subtract unwanted ones.
definition: Within a finite universe U, the desired subset A has size $|U|-|U\setminus A|$. The unwanted outcomes must be exactly the failures of the requirement.
example: Length-6 binary strings with at least one 1 number $2^6-1=63$.
confusion: Do not subtract failures from a universe with different leading-zero or repetition rules.

name: Permutation and ordered selection
quick: An arrangement in which positions matter.
definition: Full permutations of n distinct objects number n factorial. Selecting r distinct objects into labeled positions gives $P(n,r)=n!/(n-r)!$, for integers 0 at most r at most n.
example: Three offices assigned to eight people give $8\cdot7\cdot6=336$.
confusion: If repetition is allowed, the count changes to $n^r$.

name: Combination
quick: A subset of a specified size.
definition: A combination forgets the order of selection. Each r-element subset has r factorial ordered descriptions, which justifies dividing the ordered count.
example: Three people chosen from eight give $\binom83=56$ committees.
confusion: Different named roles retain order and require a different count.

name: Binomial coefficient
quick: $\binom nr$, read “n choose r,” counts r-element subsets of an n-element set.
definition: For integers $0\leq r\leq n$, its value is $n!/[r!(n-r)!]$. It counts subsets, including one empty subset and one full subset.
confusion: It is not a fraction n divided by r.

name: Pascal's identity
quick: Split subsets according to whether they contain one fixed element.
definition: For $1\leq r<n$, subsets containing the fixed element choose r-1 of the other n-1 elements; those excluding it choose r of those elements. Add the disjoint counts.
confusion: Both cases count subsets of the same original set.

name: Multiplicity
quick: The number of occurrences of a type of object.
definition: For indistinguishable objects with multiplicities $n_1,\ldots,n_k$ totaling n, visible arrangements number $n!/(n_1!\cdots n_k!)$.
example: BANANA has A three times and N twice, giving $6!/(3!2!)=60$.
confusion: Temporarily labeling identical copies creates repeated descriptions that must be removed.

name: Circular arrangement
quick: An ordering around a circle under an explicit symmetry convention.
definition: For n distinct people with rotations identified and reflections distinct, fix one person and order the other n-1 clockwise, giving (n-1) factorial arrangements.
example: Five people at an unnumbered round table give $4!=24$.
confusion: Numbered seats distinguish rotations and give a different problem.

name: Stars and bars
section: Repetition without order: distributing identical objects
quick: Encode identical-token allocations using stars separated by bars.
definition: For r identical tokens in n labeled boxes, nonnegative counts correspond to r stars and n-1 bars. Choosing bar positions gives $\binom{r+n-1}{n-1}$.
confusion: Distinct tokens retain identities and are not counted by this formula.

name: Binomial theorem
quick: Expand a power of a sum using subset-choice coefficients.
definition: In n copies of a+b, select the k factors supplying b; the other n-k supply a. This gives coefficient $\binom nk$ on $a^{n-k}b^k$.
confusion: Choose which factors supply a term, not merely how many terms appear in the final expression.

name: Pigeonhole principle
quick: Too many objects for the boxes force a shared box.
definition: Putting N objects in a positive number k of boxes forces some occupancy at least $\lceil N/k\rceil$. Otherwise the total capacity would be too small.
example: 25 people and 12 birth months force at least 3 in one month.
confusion: It gives at least the bound, not exactly the bound or the identity of the box.

name: Hash function
quick: A function assigning inputs to a fixed finite set of values.
definition: Hashes are often used to organize stored data. More distinct inputs than possible hash values force a collision by the pigeonhole principle.
example: 1001 distinct inputs and 1000 output values force two inputs with the same hash.
confusion: A forced collision is an existence result, not a probability estimate.

name: Double-counting proof
section: Counting the same set in two ways
quick: Count one finite collection by two methods to prove an identity.
definition: Define the objects precisely, including any distinguished element or named role. Both totals must count exactly that same collection.
example: Committee-and-chair pairs can be counted by choosing the committee first or the chair first.
confusion: This proof method differs from accidentally counting an outcome twice.

name: Alphabet
quick: The set of symbols allowed in a string.
definition: An alphabet specifies which individual symbols may occupy each position. A finite string over that alphabet is an ordered sequence of those symbols. Restrictions such as no repeated symbols are additional conditions, not part of the alphabet itself.
example: The alphabet {A, B, C} allows strings AB and BA, which are different. If repetition is permitted, AA is allowed too. The binary alphabet consists of 0 and 1.
confusion: A mathematical alphabet need not consist of letters. It can contain digits or other distinct symbols; a string retains their order.
